opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most exciting shifts in how we approach meta-learning, and it's worth situating it historically. For a long time, if you wanted to discover new RL algorithms automatically, you had two broad options. One was to meta-learn a black-box function: parameterize the update rule or the loss with a neural network and train it end to end across a distribution of environments. We did a fair bit of this with learned policy optimization, where you meta-learn the drift function inside a mirror-descent-style objective. That works, and it can find surprisingly good things, but the result is opaque and often brittle when you move outside the training distribution. The other option was classical program search or genetic programming over symbolic expressions, which gives you interpretable outputs but suffers from a combinatorially enormous search space. Most random mutations are garbage.

What large language models change is the prior over that program space. An LLM has read essentially the whole literature: every PPO implementation, every paper on advantage estimation, trust regions, entropy regularization. So when you ask it to propose a modification to a loss function, it isn't sampling uniformly. It proposes things that look like plausible research ideas. Effectively you get a mutation operator that already knows what a sensible algorithm looks like, and that collapses the search problem dramatically.

A nice example is the work we did with Chris Lu and colleagues on discovering preference optimization objectives, where the LLM proposes candidate loss functions as code, we evaluate them, feed the results back, and it iterates. It found objectives that were competitive with or better than hand-designed ones, and crucially you can read the code. You can look at it and say, oh, this is blending a logistic and an exponential term in a particular way, and then reason about why that helps. That interpretability is a huge deal, because it closes the loop back to human understanding rather than just giving you a magic black box.

That said, I'd caution against overclaiming. A few things worry me. First, the LLM's prior is also a bias. It's very good at recombining known ideas and much less obviously good at proposing things that are genuinely out of distribution relative to human research. So there's a real question of whether we're discovering new algorithms or doing a very efficient literature-informed hyperparameter search in program space. Second, evaluation is the bottleneck. In RL especially, evaluations are noisy and expensive, and if your fitness signal is a handful of seeds on a handful of environments, you will overfit. You'll find programs that exploit quirks of your benchmark. This is why I care so much about fast, hardware-accelerated environments in JAX: when you can run thousands of training runs in minutes on a single GPU, the outer loop becomes feasible at a scale where the signal actually means something.

Third, and this is the deeper point, the most interesting version of this isn't just LLMs proposing RL algorithms, it's the open-ended version, where the system also proposes the environments, the curricula, the problems worth solving. Algorithm discovery against a fixed benchmark is ultimately bounded by that benchmark. If you want something like an automated scientist, it has to be able to decide what's interesting, generate new challenges, and accumulate an archive of stepping stones. That's where I think the real leverage is, and also where the hardest open problems are.

So my short answer is: LLM-guided program search makes algorithm discovery practical and interpretable in a way it wasn't before, but whether it gives us genuinely novel science rather than clever recombination depends on getting the evaluation infrastructure and the open-endedness right.

r001.rationale: It contrasts black-box learned update rules with symbolic program search and describes LLM-guided search over candidate algorithm code as an alternative.

r002.rationale: It says the LLM proposes code changes, candidates are evaluated, and results are fed back for iteration; it also discusses evaluating across RL environments.

r003.rationale: It warns that sparse, noisy evaluations can lead the search to overfit benchmark quirks, and says scaling up evaluation helps make the signal more reliable.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So I think the honest answer is that it changes the game in a way that's a bit uncomfortable for people like me who spent years hand-designing RL algorithms.

For a long time, the discovery process in RL has basically been: a human has an intuition, writes down an objective or an update rule, runs it on a handful of benchmarks, and if it beats the baseline you write the paper. That's an incredibly narrow search. You're exploring a tiny corner of the space of possible algorithms, and the corner is defined by what fits in a human head and what looks elegant in a NeurIPS submission.

What we started doing with things like learned policy gradients, and then more recently with LLM-driven approaches, is to say: let's treat the algorithm itself as the object we're searching over. Early on we did this with neural networks parameterising the update rule, meta-learning the loss. That worked, but you end up with a black box. You've discovered something, but you can't read it, you can't reason about it, and it's hard to tell whether it generalises or just overfit to your training distribution of environments.

The shift with LLM-guided search is that the search space becomes code. The LLM proposes a candidate objective or update rule as an actual program, we evaluate it empirically across a distribution of tasks, and then we feed the results back and ask for improvements. And the crucial thing is that the output is interpretable. You get something you can read, and in many cases something you can actually analyse. In our discovered policy optimisation work, for example, the thing that came out was a fairly simple modification to the PPO objective, and once you look at it you can tell a story about why it works, in terms of how it handles trust region violations.

So I see three things happening. First, the search becomes much broader than human intuition allows, because the LLM has absorbed essentially the entire literature and can recombine ideas in ways no individual researcher would think to try. Second, the search is grounded, because every proposal gets tested, so you're not just getting plausible-sounding text, you're getting things that survive contact with the environment. And third, you keep the human in the loop at the level that matters, which is understanding. The human role moves from designing algorithms to designing the search: picking the task distributions, deciding what we're optimising for, and then interpreting what comes out.

The caveat I'd give is that the task distribution is everything. If you search over a narrow set of environments you'll discover algorithms that are great on those and terrible elsewhere, and the LLM is very good at finding those exploits. So a lot of the real work is in building meta-training distributions that force generality. Done right, though, I genuinely think this is how most RL algorithms will be discovered in a few years, and the interesting scientific question becomes understanding why the discovered ones work.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts earlier neural-network-parameterized, black-box update rules with searching over candidate algorithms written as code.

r002.rationale: It says the LLM proposes program candidates, evaluates them across tasks, then uses the results to request improvements.

r003.rationale: It warns that narrow task distributions produce algorithms that exploit those environments and says distributions must be designed to promote generality.

astra-6.text:
I think the exciting possibility is that we can search over the learning algorithm itself. Instead of fixing an update rule and tuning its hyperparameters, you can represent that update rule as a program and use an LLM to propose changes. Then you actually run those programs and measure whether they produce better learning.

That gives you a loop where the language model supplies plausible candidates, but experiments determine which ones survive. The model doesn’t have to know in advance why a particular modification will work. It needs to propose enough useful variations that the search can make progress.

The difficult part is deciding what counts as progress. Reinforcement learning results are noisy, and if you search long enough against a small set of environments, you can discover something that exploits your evaluation procedure rather than a broadly useful algorithm. So held-out tasks, multiple seeds, and fair compute budgets become central to the discovery process.

What I’d find most interesting is a compact program that works across quite different settings and that we can subsequently understand. You discover an update rule experimentally, then ask: what principle is it exploiting? That could make automated search a source of new scientific hypotheses, as well as better-performing algorithms.

r001.rationale: The response proposes searching over update-rule programs, but does not frame this as an alternative to black-box function approximators.

r002.rationale: It says an LLM proposes program changes, which are run and evaluated for better learning, including across environments and held-out tasks.

r003.rationale: It warns that extended search on a small set of environments can exploit the evaluation procedure and recommends held-out tasks and multiple seeds.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the exciting possibility is that we can start searching over the learning algorithm itself. Normally, we pick a parameterized family—say, a particular policy gradient update—and then tune its hyperparameters. But there’s a much larger space of possible programs that take experience and produce an update. An LLM can propose changes in that space, and experiments can tell us whether those changes actually help.

The crucial thing is that the language model isn’t the judge. It proposes a candidate; you run it, measure performance, and feed that evidence back into the search. That gives you a way to combine useful structure from existing code and ideas with an objective grounded in interaction with an environment.

But you have to be very careful about what you’re selecting for. If you evaluate thousands of candidates on a small set of environments, you can discover something that exploits the benchmark rather than a broadly useful learning principle. So held-out tasks, multiple seeds, and accounting for the compute spent searching become really important.

For me, the interesting outcome isn’t just a program that gets a higher score. It’s a program we can then study: what is it doing differently, which parts matter, and can we extract a simpler principle? That could make this a powerful tool for discovery, provided we do the scientific work after the search as well.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts searching over learning-update programs with choosing a parameterized update and tuning hyperparameters, but does not identify black-box function approximators as the alternative.

r002.rationale: It says an LLM proposes program changes, then experiments measure their performance and feed that evidence back into the search.

r003.rationale: It warns that searching thousands of candidates on few environments can overfit to the benchmark and recommends held-out tasks.
